summary: Nuxt: Server-side route rules (`redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr`) are skipped for case-variant paths when routing is case-insensitive
description:
## Impact

With the default `router.options.sensitive: false`, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so `/Admin` renders the same page as `/admin`. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes ([GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47), [GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9)) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as `appMiddleware`. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

- `redirect`: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }`, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
- `headers`: per-route response headers, including security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` or `X-Frame-Options`, were not sent.
- `proxy`: the request was not proxied.
- `ssr: false` and `noScripts`: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, despite the rule.
- `getRouteRules(event)` (auto-imported, or from `nuxt/server`) and `matchRouteRules` from `nuxt/server` returned no rules for the case variant.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With this configuration, `/admin/secret` redirects to `/login`, but `/Admin/secret` rendered `app/pages/admin/secret.vue`.

## Mitigating factors

- Applications that set `router.options.sensitive: true` in `nuxt.config` are not affected, because their pages are only served for the exact case of the route.
- Access checks performed in server middleware, route middleware attached with `definePageMeta`, or in the page's data fetching are not affected. The issue only affects protections that rely on a server-side route rule matching the request path.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.2`, including all Nuxt 3 releases, and `@nuxt/nitro-server` `<4.6.2`.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Nuxt now resolves server-side route rules itself, decoding and case-folding both the rule keys and the request path unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, and applies the result to Nitro's `redirect`, `headers` and `proxy` handling, the renderer, and the `getRouteRules` / `matchRouteRules` helpers.

When routing is case-insensitive, patched releases change some behaviour:

- Route rules also apply to case variants of server API routes. For example, `/API/x` now matches a `/api/**` `proxy` or `headers` rule.
- Rule keys that differ only in letter case now resolve to the same path on the server, and the later key takes precedence.

The following are not changed by this fix:

- `cache` and `swr` response caching is attached to server routes by Nitro's router, which matches case-sensitively. A case variant is still rendered with its route rules applied, but its response is not cached.
- Rules that a deployment preset compiles into platform configuration (for example Vercel's `config.json` or Netlify's `_redirects` and `_headers`) are matched by the platform. Once a request reaches the Nuxt server, the rules are applied as described above.
- If `sensitive` is set only in `app/router.options.ts`, the server follows the `nuxt.config` value. In that configuration route rules can only apply to more paths, never fewer.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Set `router: { options: { sensitive: true } }` in `nuxt.config`, so pages are only served for the exact case of their route.
2. Alternatively, enforce access control in server middleware or route middleware rather than relying on a `redirect` route rule, and set security headers for every response rather than per route.

summary: Nuxt server islands render `useHeadSafe` input without sanitisation
description:
## Impact

`useHeadSafe` restricts head input to an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. For example, `bodyAttrs` is limited to `class` and `style`, event handler attributes are removed, and `<script>` tags are only kept for JSON types.

When `useHeadSafe` is called inside a server island (a `.server.vue` component or page, or a component rendered with `<NuxtIsland>`), the island renderer serialises the raw input of every head entry into the island response without the option that marks it as safe input. `<NuxtIsland>` then pushes that input into the page's head as a regular entry, both during server rendering and when hydrating or refetching on the client.

As a result, input that `useHeadSafe` would normally strip (such as `bodyAttrs.onload` or executable `<script>` content) is rendered into the page. If an application passes user-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island, an attacker who controls that data can achieve stored cross-site scripting on the application's origin.

```vue
<!-- components/AuthorMeta.server.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const { data: author } = await useFetch('/api/author')
// author.value.head is user-authored, e.g. { bodyAttrs: { onload: '...' } }
useHeadSafe(author.value.head)
</script>
```

## Mitigating factors

- Server components are experimental. They are only active when the application defines a `.server.vue` component or page, or enables `experimental.componentIslands` and renders `<NuxtIsland>`.
- Exploitation requires the application to pass attacker-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island. `useHeadSafe` called from regular (non-island) components and pages is not affected.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `>=3.13.0`, when head support for server islands was introduced. Nuxt 2 is not affected.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.2`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Patched releases apply Unhead's safe input filtering to `useHeadSafe` entries on the server before they are added to the island response, so `islandResponse.head` (including what `render:island` hooks see) only contains input that `useHeadSafe` allows.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.2`. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

1. Call `useHeadSafe` with untrusted input from a regular component or page rather than from inside a server island.
2. Alternatively, validate untrusted head input against your own allowlist before passing it to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island.

summary: Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26: a `javascript:` URL prefixed with an ASCII control character executes from `<NuxtLink>` when `pages` is disabled
description:
## Impact

An application that renders `<NuxtLink :to="...">` with a value it does not control can be made to render an anchor whose `href` executes script in the application's origin when clicked.

This is an incomplete fix for [GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26) (CVE-2026-53722). It only affects applications running without a `pages/` directory, where `pages` resolves to `false` and Nuxt registers its own router in place of vue-router. Applications using vue-router are not affected.

Prefixing `javascript:` with an ASCII C0 control character, for example `%01`, meant the value was not recognised as having a protocol. It was classified as an internal route and so never reached the protocol check added in GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26, and the router used for `pages: false` passed it through to the rendered `href` unchanged. Browsers strip the leading control character and run the result as a script URL.

Both `<NuxtLink custom>` and the default anchor are affected, and the `href` is present in the server-rendered HTML.

## Mitigating factors

- The application must have `pages` disabled (no `pages/` directory, or `pages: false`).
- The application must bind untrusted input to `:to`.
- A victim must click the rendered link.

## Affected versions

`nuxt` `<4.6.0`, including all Nuxt 3 releases. Versions before `4.4.7` and `3.21.7` are also affected by GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26.

## Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.0`. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Anchor `href` values are now checked for script-capable protocols wherever they are rendered, including the router used when `pages` is disabled. Protocol detection also moved to the platform `URL` parser, so a URL is classified the same way the browser will read it.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `nuxt@4.6.0` or later. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3, validate values before binding them to `:to`, for example by rejecting anything that is not a path beginning with a single `/`.

summary: Nuxt: Route rules are matched against the raw request path, so a percent-encoded segment can bypass `appMiddleware` on dynamic and catch-all routes
description:
### Summary

Nuxt compared `routeRules` keys against the raw request path, without decoding percent-encoding, while the router decodes parameters when it resolves a route. A request whose path is percent-encoded can therefore resolve to a page while failing to match the route rule meant to protect it, so the rule's `appMiddleware` never runs, including during server rendering.

### Impact

For a page served through a dynamic or catch-all route, an attacker can percent-encode a character in the path to skip the rule:

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/users/admin': { appMiddleware: 'auth' },
  },
})
```

Requesting `/users/%61dmin` still renders `app/pages/users/[id].vue` with `id` decoded to `admin`, but the rule keyed `/users/admin` does not match, so `auth` does not run and the server renders and returns the gated page to an unauthenticated visitor. No privileges and no user interaction are required, and only ASCII characters are involved.

Purely static ASCII routes are not affected: static segments are matched without decoding, so a request for `/%61dmin` does not resolve to the page registered at `/admin` and 404s instead of rendering.

The rule keys affected are the ones carried in the app manifest and consumed by the app: `appMiddleware`, `redirect`, `appLayout`, `ssr`, `prerender`, and the payload flags derived from `cache`, `isr` and `swr`.

If you have pinned or overridden dependency versions below what your Nuxt release declares, a release outside the affected ranges can still be exposed, so do not conclude from a single reproduction that you are unaffected.

### Patches

Releases from `4.4.4` and `3.21.4` are not affected, because their dependency floor requires a version of the underlying HTTP layer that normalises percent-encoding in the request path before routing, which removes the mismatch in a default install.

The comparison itself is fixed in `nuxt@4.5.2` and `nuxt@3.21.11`: route-rule keys and lookup paths are now decoded (and, unless `router.options.sensitive` is set, case-folded) before they are compared. Reserved escapes such as `%2F` are left encoded, so decoding cannot introduce extra path segments, and paths that cannot be decoded are matched verbatim. Upgrading to those releases is recommended, since it fixes the comparison rather than relying on a dependency to normalise the input, and it also restores route rules for pages whose paths contain non-ASCII characters.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not rely on a `routeRules` key alone to protect a route. Attach the middleware to the page itself, which binds it to the resolved route rather than to the raw path string:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
definePageMeta({ middleware: 'auth' })
</script>
```

### Credits

Thanks to @sushi-gif, whose report that route rules keyed with non-ASCII paths never match the routes generated for those pages prompted the review that found this issue.

summary: Electron: SameSite cookie restrictions are not applied to windows opened from links
description:
### Impact

Pages opened into a new window from a link were loaded as if the app itself had navigated there rather than the page that contained the link, so the request was treated as same-site: `SameSite=Strict` cookies were sent and `Sec-Fetch-Site` did not identify the initiating page. Content shown in the app could use this to make a credentialed top-level request to another site that relies on SameSite cookies as a CSRF defence.

Apps are only affected if they load untrusted content and allow it to open new windows. Apps that deny new windows from untrusted content with `setWindowOpenHandler` are not affected.

### Workarounds

Return `{ action: 'deny' }` from `setWindowOpenHandler` for windows opened by untrusted content.

### Fixed Versions

* `45.0.0-alpha.6`
* `44.3.0`
* `43.7.0`
* `42.11.3`

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

Deny the `pointerLock` permission for web contents that embed untrusted frames.

summary: fastify is vulnerable to header validation bypass via case-sensitive propertyNames
description:
### Impact

Fastify lowercases header names in a `headers` schema before compilation, because Node.js stores request header names in lowercase. This normalization does not reach the header names held in a `propertyNames` subschema's `enum` and `const`. A header-name deny-list written in the canonical header case, such as `propertyNames: { not: { enum: ['X-Debug-Override'] } }`, therefore never matches the lowercased request headers, and the forbidden header reaches the handler. Any application that uses a `propertyNames` deny-list or allow-list to constrain request header names does not get the constraint it expects. The same rule written in lowercase works, and the `not: { required: [...] }` form is unaffected, so this is a gap in the built-in normalization rather than a wrong schema. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-84428 ([GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/security/advisories/GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58)), whose normalization covered header names used as property keys but not those used as values inside `propertyNames`.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to fastify `5.12.6` or later, which lowercases header names held in `enum` and `const` inside a `propertyNames` subschema so they match the lowercased request headers. Header-name constraints that cannot be normalized automatically, regular expressions (`propertyNames` `pattern` and `patternProperties` keys) and a `$ref` used inside `propertyNames`, are documented and, for the `$ref` case, warned at startup (`FSTSEC003`). Author those to match the lowercased request headers.

### Workarounds

Write the `propertyNames` header-name constraint in lowercase (for example `enum: ['x-debug-override']`), or enforce the header check in an `onRequest` or `preValidation` hook instead of the schema.

summary: toml-node: Prototype pollution: parsing a TOML document can write to Object.prototype
description:
### Summary
CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through __proto__ key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

### Details
Three gaps compose. All line numbers are `lib/compiler.js` in 5.0.0.

**1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous.** `quoteDottedString()` quotes a segment only when it contains a `.`, and never escapes a `"` inside the segment:

```js
287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }
```

So the key path `['x.y']` and the key path `['"x', 'y"']` both render as the string `"x.y"`. This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

**2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard.** `addTableArray()` walks `assignedPaths` / `valueAssignments` with `isSameOrSubPath()` over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

**3. The descent in `assign()` has no owned-container check.** `deepRef()` applies `isOwnedContainer()` only to intermediate segments (`lib/compiler.js:265`, `:273`) and returns the final container unchecked. `assign()` then walks it with only a shape test:

```js
 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;
```

A TOML datetime is a `Date`. It satisfies `typeof target[k] === "object"` and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a `Date` has a live prototype chain to `Object.prototype`.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a `Date` and then walk `__proto__.__proto__` to `Object.prototype`.

```bash
mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0
```

```toml
# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z
[['"b']]
["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"
```

Line 1 defines a key whose rendered path is `"b.c"` and whose value is a `Date`.
Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard.
Line 3 re-enters that key, so the current table is now the `Date`.
Line 4 walks `Date` → `Date.prototype` → `Object.prototype`.

```js
// poc.js
const toml = require('toml');
const fs = require('fs');

console.log('before:', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
toml.parse(fs.readFileSync('poc.toml', 'utf8'));
console.log('after: ', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
console.log('Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") =', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'));
console.log('JSON.parse("{}").polluted =', JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{}').polluted));
```

```
$ node poc.js
before: undefined
after:  "yes"
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") = true
JSON.parse("{}").polluted = "yes"
```

The payload sets a single harmless marker property. The last line shows the property is visible on an object this code never touched.

A useful control: the same document without line 2 (the guard-clearing header) is correctly rejected on 4.1.2 and later, which confirms the clearing step is what is load-bearing.

### Impact

Any application that parses a TOML document from an untrusted source is affected — a configuration file uploaded by a user, a manifest from a third-party package or repository, a document posted to an API. Prototype pollution of this kind commonly escalates to authentication or authorization bypass, denial of service, and in applications with a suitable gadget, remote code execution, because every object in the process inherits the injected property.

Suggested fix: in `assign()`, apply the same check the intermediate descent already uses — after `target = target[k]`, reject when `!isOwnedContainer(target)`. Equivalently, apply `isOwnedContainer` to the value `deepRef()` returns. Separately, `quoteDottedString()` should escape `"` inside a segment so that distinct key paths cannot render to the same string.

summary: toml-node: Quadratic-complexity DoS via many array-of-tables headers in toml.parse()
description:
## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via many
array-of-tables (`[[name]]`) headers. `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js` rescans two
entire bookkeeping Sets on every `[[name]]` header without pruning unrelated or distinct
entries, so a document containing n such headers costs O(n²) compiler work. A ~321KB document
of 20,000 distinct-named `[[name]]` blocks takes ~10.3 seconds to parse — a completely
ordinary-looking TOML shape (a flat settings block plus one or more array-of-tables sections),
not a contrived edge case. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously fixed
stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) and requires no key nesting or dotted keys at all.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Function: `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected function is
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation. Every
`[[name]]` (array-of-tables) header is routed (`reduce()`, `lib/compiler.js:43`) to
`addTableArray()` (`lib/compiler.js:218-245`), which performs two full linear scans on every
call:

```js
assignedPaths.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) assignedPaths.delete(p);
});
valueAssignments.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) valueAssignments.delete(p);
});
```
(`lib/compiler.js:228-233`)

`assignedPaths` and `valueAssignments` accumulate one entry per top-level key/table/array path
ever assigned in the entire document. Each scan prunes only entries matching the *currently
reopened* path via `isSameOrSubPath()` (`lib/compiler.js:319-321`: `path === prefix ||
path.indexOf(prefix + ".") === 0`); anything else — an unrelated top-level key, or simply a
*different* array-of-tables name — is never removed and is rescanned in full on every
subsequent `[[name]]` header for the rest of the parse. `Set.prototype.forEach` has no early
exit, so this is unconditionally O(current Set size) on every call, giving O(n²) total work
for n such headers.

## Proof of Concept

The sharpest reproduction needs no unrelated keys at all — just N array-of-tables headers with
N *distinct* names, since nothing is ever pruned when no name repeats:

```js
const toml = require('toml');

function distinctArrayHeaders(n) {
  let out = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out += `[[a${i}]]\nv = 1\n`;
  return out;
}

// ~321 KB input -- takes ~10.3 seconds
toml.parse(distinctArrayHeaders(20000));
```

Measured timings (Node, direct execution against this repo):

| Variant | n | input size | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| N distinct-named `[[name]]` headers, no unrelated keys | 20,000 | 321 KB | 10.3 s |
| Same N with all-same-name headers (self-pruning, control) | 20,000 | 240 KB | 78 ms |
| M unrelated top-level keys + N same-name `[[name]]` headers | M=N=32,000 | 906 KB | 42.3 s |

The ~130x gap between the distinct-name and same-name cases at identical N and comparable
input size isolates the mechanism precisely: the bug is unbounded Set growth from never-pruned
entries, not string length or any other confound. A product-law check (varying M and N
independently in the mixed variant) further confirmed genuine O(M·N) complexity.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — this synchronous, multi-second-to-tens-of-seconds compile blocks
the entire process event loop, standard uncontested Node.js behavior. The triggering document
shape — flat top-level config keys plus one or more array-of-tables sections (e.g. a `[db]`
settings block plus a `[[servers]]` list) — is unremarkable, common real-world TOML, not an
edge case. No authentication or special access is required; only the ability to get one TOML
string parsed by an application using this library.

## Suggested remediation

Avoid scanning the entire `assignedPaths`/`valueAssignments` Sets on every `[[name]]` header.
Index entries by their top-level path segment (e.g. a `Map<string, Set<string>>` keyed by the
first key component) so `addTableArray()` only ever scans the bucket relevant to the path
being reopened, in time proportional to that bucket's size rather than the whole document's
accumulated path count:

```js
var assignedByRoot = new Map(); // root segment -> Set<fullPath>

function addTableArray(node) {
  var path = node.value;
  var root = path[0];
  var bucket = assignedByRoot.get(root) || new Set();
  bucket.forEach(function(p) {
    if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) bucket.delete(p);
  });
  // ...rest of addTableArray unchanged, reading/writing the per-root bucket
  // instead of the global assignedPaths/valueAssignments Sets
}
```

As with the sibling finding, an input-size or table-count limit would also help as
defense-in-depth.

summary: toml-node: Quadratic-complexity DoS via long dotted keys or table paths in toml.parse()
description:
## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via a single
long dotted key, table header, or inline-table key. A ~100KB crafted document causes a
multi-second synchronous hang; a ~200KB document crashes the Node.js process outright with an
uncatchable out-of-memory error. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously
fixed stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) — it requires no array/inline-table nesting at
all, and is confirmed unaffected by the `maxDepth` option that fixed that earlier issue.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Functions: `assign()`, `deepRef()`, `setNestedKey()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected functions are
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation.
Inside `lib/compiler.js`, three separate functions each walk a dotted key's segments in a
`for` loop and, on **every** iteration, recompute the full path-prefix string from scratch:

- `assign()` (lines 69-107, the sink at line 81): `var intermediatePath =
  makeFullPath(keys.slice(0, i + 1));` — reached for top-level dotted-key assignments like
  `a.b.c = 1`.
- `deepRef()` (lines 247-281, the sink at line 252): the identical pattern via
  `pathKey(keys.slice(0, i + 1))` — reached from table headers `[a.b.c]` and array-of-tables
  `[[a.b.c]]` via `setPath()`/`addTableArray()`.
- `setNestedKey()` (lines 184-202, the sink at line 187): the identical pattern — reached from
  inline-table dotted keys like `t = { a.b.c = 1 }`.

`keys.slice(0, i + 1)` allocates a new array of length `i`; `pathKey()`/`makeFullPath()`
(lines 311-317) then does `.map(quoteDottedString).join(".")`, also O(i). Since this runs on
every one of the `n` segments of a dotted key, total work is `O(1 + 2 + ... + n) = O(n²)`, not
`O(n)`. The string is computed unconditionally on the happy path (only ever *used* if an error
is about to be thrown), so there is no early exit that makes this cheap in practice.

No limit exists anywhere on dotted-key segment count: `dot_ended_table_key_part+` and
`inline_dot_key_part+` in `src/toml.pegjs` (lines 122, 311) are unbounded `+` repetitions,
parsed iteratively rather than through the grammar's `value` rule — so the existing
`MAX_DEPTH`/`maxDepth` nesting guard (`src/toml.pegjs:141-151`, enforced in the generated
`lib/parser.js:1022`) does not apply to key length at all. We confirmed this directly: setting
`options.maxDepth: 1` (the strictest possible value) against a 16,000-segment key produced no
measurable timing difference from the unrestricted case.

## Proof of Concept

```js
const toml = require('toml');

// n-segment dotted key: "k0.k1.k2. ... .k{n-1} = 1"
function segKey(n) {
  const parts = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) parts.push('k' + i);
  return parts.join('.') + ' = 1\n';
}

// ~100.9 KB input -- takes ~6.6-6.8 seconds
toml.parse(segKey(16000));

// ~200 KB input -- crashes the Node process:
// "FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit - JavaScript heap out of memory"
toml.parse(segKey(32000));
```

Measured timings (Node v22, direct execution against this repo):

| n (segments) | input size | time |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | ~4.9 KB | 34 ms |
| 8,000 | ~46.9 KB | 1.6 s |
| 16,000 | ~100.9 KB | 6.8 s |
| 32,000 | ~200 KB | **process crash (OOM)** |

Doubling `n` from 8,000→16,000 roughly quadruples runtime (~4.2x), the signature of O(n²)
rather than the expected O(n) (~2x). Independently reproduced with the identical scaling
signature for the table-header variant (`[k0. ... .k15999]`, exercising `deepRef()`) and the
inline-table variant (`t = { k0. ... .k15999 = 1 }`, exercising `setNestedKey()`).

We also generalized this into a property-based fuzzing harness (fast-check, run under Node)
that automatically tests the "doubling input size should not more than roughly double parse
time" invariant across 12 structural dimensions of the grammar/compiler; it independently
re-flags all three code paths above on every run, with no additional dimension confirmed
vulnerable after follow-up investigation. The harness is available on request.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — a synchronous multi-second-to-crashing `parse()` call blocks the
entire event loop of the process calling it, stalling every other request/operation that
process is handling, not just the attacker's own. At the upper end this is not merely a hang:
an uncaught, process-terminating out-of-memory crash from a ~200KB attacker-supplied string is
a full denial of service requiring no authentication — just the ability to get one string
parsed by an application using this library (config upload, API request body, imported
manifest, or any of this library's intended use cases).

## Suggested remediation

Build the path prefix as an incrementally-extended string as the loop walks each segment
(append one already-quoted segment per iteration to a running string) instead of re-slicing an
array and re-joining the entire prefix from scratch on every iteration. For example, in
`assign()`:

```js
function assign(node) {
  var keys = node.key;
  var value = node.value;
  var off = node.offset;
  if (!Array.isArray(keys)) keys = [keys];
  var reduced = reduceValueNode(value);

  var target = context;
  var pathStr = pathKey(currentPath); // computed once, not per segment
  for (var i = 0; i < keys.length - 1; i++) {
    var k = keys[i];
    var quotedK = quoteDottedString(k);
    var intermediatePath = pathStr ? pathStr + "." + quotedK : quotedK; // O(new segment), not O(i)
    pathStr = intermediatePath;
    // ...same conditional logic as today, using intermediatePath
    target = target[k];
  }
  // ...
}
```

The identical treatment applies to `deepRef()` and `setNestedKey()`. As defense-in-depth,
consider also capping total key-segment count or overall input size, the same way `maxDepth`
already caps nesting.

summary: toml-node: Uncontrolled resource consumption (CPU DoS) via unbounded-length integer literals in toml.parse()
description:
### Summary
`toml.parse()` converts integer literals (hex, octal, binary, and decimal) to `BigInt` without first bounding the length of the digit sequence. Since `BigInt(string)` construction from a very long numeric string runs in super-linear time, a single small, well-formed TOML document containing one long integer literal can pin a Node.js process's event loop at 100% CPU for several seconds — a denial of service for any application that parses attacker-supplied or third-party TOML. No authentication or complex crafting is required.

### Details
In `lib/parser.js`, the grammar actions that build integer nodes call `BigInt()` directly on the matched digit text, with no upper bound on its length:

- `lib/parser.js:326` — hex: `BigInt('0x' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:327` — octal: `BigInt('0o' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:328` — binary: `BigInt('0b' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:329` — decimal: `BigInt(stripUnderscores(text))`

The parser does enforce a nesting-depth limit (`MAX_DEPTH`, default 500, `lib/parser.js:4343`) to guard against stack overflow from deeply nested arrays/inline tables (per GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf). However, that guard only bounds *structural nesting* — it does not bound the length of a single scalar token.

The subsequent 64-bit range check in `lib/compiler.js` (`reduceInteger`, lines 143–150, comparing against `INT64_MIN` / `INT64_MAX` defined at lines 3–4) happens **after** the expensive `BigInt()` conversion has already completed. It therefore provides no protection against this cost — the CPU time is already spent by the time the value is rejected as out of range.

### PoC

```js
const toml = require('toml');

const N = 5_000_000; // ~5 MB request body
const doc = 'x = 0x' + 'f'.repeat(N);

const start = Date.now();
try {
  toml.parse(doc); // eventually throws "outside the 64-bit signed integer range" —
                    // but only after the costly conversion has run
} catch (e) {}

console.log('elapsed:', Date.now() - start, 'ms');
```

**Measured results:**

| Digits (hex) | Approx. payload size | Parse time |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 200,000 | ~200 KB | 141 ms |
| 400,000 | ~400 KB | 276 ms |
| 800,000 | ~800 KB | 685 ms |
| 1,600,000 | ~1.6 MB | 1,761 ms |
| 5,000,000 | ~5 MB | 6,061 ms |

Growth is clearly super-linear. The same behavior reproduces for plain decimal literals (3,000,000 `'9'` digits → ~6.3 s).

### Impact
Any application that calls `toml.parse()` on untrusted or third-party input — config upload endpoints, CI/CD tools ingesting user-supplied `.toml` files, package managers, linters, editors/language servers — is exposed.

During the conversion, the event loop is fully blocked. In a typical single-threaded Node.js server this stalls **all** concurrent request handling, not just the request containing the malicious payload. A single ~5 MB request is sufficient to cause several seconds of full CPU denial of service.

**Suggested fix:** Reject digit sequences above a reasonable length *before* calling `BigInt()`, analogous to the existing `maxDepth` option. A 64-bit signed integer requires at most 20 decimal digits or 16 hex digits, so any digit sequence significantly longer than that is guaranteed to fail the existing range check anyway, and can be rejected with a cheap `.length` comparison instead of paying for the full `BigInt` conversion.

summary: Storybook dev server vulnerable to code injection from the local network
description:
**Summary:** The Storybook dev server exposes its WebSocket authentication token to any client that can load its HTML pages. Any host on a LAN can open a Storybook app by IP address, and therefore obtain the token. The WebSocket can be used to inject code into story files or to create new files. Under the right circumstances, an attacker can execute code on the machine of a developer connected on the same LAN.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server whilst connected on an untrusted local network, or to a WiFi access point posing as a trusted network. The impact of this advisory is more important if you have the Vitest addon installed and are using an old version of Vitest.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server in an environment that other devices on your network cannot reach (e.g. a container that does not publish the Storybook port, or publishes it only on `127.0.0.1`)
- You run a dev server whilst connected to a trusted local network
- You serve a built version of Storybook on your machine

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

- 11.0.0-alpha.6
- 10.6.2
- 9.1.21
- 8.6.19

### Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, this document explains how to fall back to the previous behavior.

#### Storybook now only listens on `127.0.0.1` by default

By default, the Storybook dev server no longer binds to all network interfaces on your machine. It only binds to the loopback address `127.0.0.1`. You can still open it at `http://localhost:6006`. This prevents other devices on the same network from seeing your Storybook server.

To share a Storybook with others, consider publishing it to Chromatic (free). To share it on a LAN without exposing the dev server, build a static Storybook with `storybook build` and serve the output folder with any static file server.

To share a live Storybook running in dev mode, you can use the `--host` CLI option to bind to the LAN IP you want to share Storybook on, e.g. `storybook dev --host 192.168.0.110`. Host and origin validation stays enabled with this option. If you use `--host 0.0.0.0` instead, also set `core.allowedHosts` to the hostnames you will use. Without it, host and origin validation is disabled, and Storybook shows a warning and asks you to confirm before it starts.

Consider using a firewall to restrict incoming packets to known colleague IPs, and avoid using `--host` on an untrusted WiFi network.

#### The Vitest addon now disables `browser.api.allowWrite` and `browser.api.allowExec`

Storybook no longer allows code running in Vitest Browser mode to write to the developer’s machine or execute other processes. In the unlikely scenario that you rely on this capability in your tests, you can manually re-enable these APIs in your Vitest config.

#### The `saveStoryRequest` event validates input more strictly

Storybook strengthened input validation in `saveStoryRequest`, so addons and the Storybook UI can now only write serialized args and story titles. It is no longer possible to exploit input validation weaknesses to e.g. write `play` functions with a custom addon.

If you develop an addon that writes or edits files on users’ behalf, reach out to the Storybook team to get advice on security best practice.

## Disclosure timeline

On August 19th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure showing that the WebSocket token can be stolen by an attacker sharing a LAN with a Storybook dev server.

The disclosure identified several actions an attacker can do. An attacker can bypass input validation to write a payload in a story file.

They can then trigger a test run via the WebSocket. If the Vitest addon is installed, the payload can exploit a Vitest API to write other files, with more exploit logic to the user’s filesystem.

Depending on the exploit content, where the file is written, and what software the developer uses, that exploit could then be executed.

summary: Astro: Reflected/Stored XSS via unescaped <script>/<style> tag content in JSX/MDX rendering
description:
## Summary

Astro's JSX and MDX rendering pipeline treated string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as trusted HTML. When a dynamic value was passed through a JSX expression, such as `<script>{value}</script>`, an attacker-controlled value containing `</script>` or `</style>` could terminate the element and inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript.

Other JSX expression contexts escaped dynamic strings automatically. This behavior was limited to `<script>` and `<style>` children rendered through Astro's `astro:jsx` renderer, including MDX components.

## Details

The affected rendering paths marked all string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as safe HTML, without distinguishing literal content generated by the compiler from dynamic expression values. An application was vulnerable when attacker-controlled data, such as a query parameter or CMS field, was interpolated directly into one of these elements.

For example, a value containing `</script><script>alert(1)</script>` passed to `<script>{value}</script>` was emitted without escaping. The browser interpreted the first closing tag as markup and executed the injected script.

The fix preserves raw rendering for literal script and style content while escaping dynamic string children like other JSX expression values.

## Impact

Affected applications could be vulnerable to reflected or stored cross-site scripting. Exploitation required an application to pass attacker-controlled data directly as a dynamic child of a `<script>` or `<style>` element in MDX or through the `astro:jsx` runtime. Successful exploitation allowed arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser under the application's origin.

## Patches

This issue is patched in `astro@7.3.2`.

## Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted dynamic values directly into `<script>` or `<style>` element children. Applications that cannot upgrade should validate and contextually encode these values before rendering them.

## Credit

Reported by [@RKasai127](https://github.com/RKasai127).

summary: GraphQL Tools: Prototype pollution in mergeIncrementalResult via non-primitive path segments
description:
## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/utils` (npm, `pkg:github/ardatan/graphql-tools`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `mergeIncrementalResult` / `setObjectKeyPath` (`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Prototype pollution (via unvalidated object path traversal) |
| Verified against | Source read at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b`; `master` HEAD `ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`; published npm builds 10.10.0, 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0, 12.0.1 |
| Affected versions | `@graphql-tools/utils` >= 10.10.1 through the scanned 12.0.0 source; introduced by `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` ("remove dset dependency"). 12.0.1 also reproduces. 10.10.0 does not. |
| API surface | Public, documented export (`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — no options are involved; the forbidden-key check in `setObjectKeyPath` is the only defense and it is on by default |

## Summary

`mergeIncrementalResult` merges an incremental GraphQL response part into an accumulated execution result by walking `['data', ...incrementalResult.path]` and assigning at the resolved location. `setObjectKeyPath` tries to reject dangerous segments with strict string equality against `'__proto__'`, `'constructor'` and `'prototype'` (lines 50-52 and 60-62), but it never validates that a path segment is a primitive string or number. A JSON path segment such as `["__proto__"]` is an array object, so `["__proto__"] !== '__proto__'` and the guard passes; the very next statement does `current[key]`, whose `ToPropertyKey` coercion turns that array into the string key `"__proto__"` and resolves `Object.prototype`. The following, innocuous-looking segment is then assigned directly onto `Object.prototype`.

In a consuming app, `incrementalResult` is the response part being merged — data parsed from an upstream `@defer`/`@stream` multipart or incremental-delivery response from another GraphQL server or transport. The `ExecutionResult` TypeScript annotation is not a runtime check, so a malicious, compromised, or MITM'd upstream can choose the `path` value and therefore choose global prototype keys and values in the gateway or client process.

Comparable paths through the same helper, for contrast:

- Plain string segment `"__proto__"` -> blocked by strict equality, lines 50-52 (confirmed by a control case in testing)
- Array segment `["__proto__"]` -> **unsafe: passes the guard at lines 50-52, then coerced to the `__proto__` key at lines 53-57**
- Same operation in 10.10.0 and earlier, which used `dset` -> not exploitable (0/5 attack payloads succeeded)

## Impact

A malicious incremental GraphQL response can add arbitrary properties with attacker-chosen values to `Object.prototype` in the consuming Node.js process. Because every plain object inherits from it, this can change authorization and configuration checks and the behavior of unrelated code elsewhere in the process — a networked PoC set `Object.prototype.isAdmin = true` and `Object.prototype.ownerEmail`, after which a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a freshly created `{}` returned `true`.

The delta over the safe behaviour: without this traversal flaw, a hostile upstream response can only influence the GraphQL data returned to the caller — a bounded, in-band effect. With `path: [["__proto__"], "isAdmin"]`, the write lands on `Object.prototype`, escaping the response object entirely and affecting objects created later and code that never touches the response.

Scoring note: **this report deliberately carries no CVSS vector.** No score was produced for it, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow — specifically whether it merges incremental results from an upstream it does not control, and how much it relies on inherited defaults. Consumers who are **not** affected: anything on `@graphql-tools/utils` 10.10.0 or earlier (the `dset`-based implementation blocked all tested payloads); processes that freeze `Object.prototype`; and consumers that runtime-validate incremental `path` segments to primitives before calling the helper. Note also that `graphql-tools`' own production code does not call `mergeIncrementalResult` directly — it is exported for consumers assembling incremental transport results.

## Preconditions

1. The consumer calls the public `mergeIncrementalResult` helper on incremental payloads received from another GraphQL server or other untrusted transport. No special options are needed.
2. The incremental payload is not runtime-validated to contain only primitive string/number `path` segments before the call. This is the default: `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55` exports the helper directly, with no runtime validation and no documented warning, and the behaviour is not documented as a caller responsibility.
3. The attacker can return a malformed incremental `path` value — i.e. controls, has compromised, or can MITM the upstream subgraph/transport.
4. The process has not frozen `Object.prototype`.

This requires **no** non-standard usage, monkey-patching, or unusual configuration: the documented happy path of the exported helper is affected. The only defense present in the code is the strict-equality forbidden-key check added at lines 50 and 60, which itself shows the author treats these path segments as untrusted input. No documentation warning about the trust requirement was found (documentation review is limited to the exported symbol at `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`; a broader docs audit is **not verified**).

## Data flow

1. **Source** — the attacker-controlled `incrementalResult.path`, taken from the object passed to the public merge helper, is spread into the key path: `const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:12`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L12)).
2. **Propagation** — `setObjectKeyPath` compares the unvalidated segment against the forbidden strings with `===` only; a non-primitive segment is never equal to any of them, so it passes unchanged ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:48-52`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L48-L52)).
3. **Sink** — `current[key]` performs `ToPropertyKey` coercion, turning the array segment `["__proto__"]` into the key `"__proto__"` and resolving `Object.prototype`; the following segment is then assigned on that resolved object: `current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:53-57`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L53-L57), sink at [`:59-64`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L59-L64)).
4. **Reachability** — the entry point is the public API `mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult })`, exported directly at [`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/index.ts#L55) for consumers that assemble incremental transport results. Testing confirmed the `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.

## Vulnerable code

`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`, lines 12-64 at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b` (extract; the `...` markers are elisions of intervening lines, not source text):

```ts
const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];
...
const key = keyPath[i];
if (key === '__proto__' || key === 'constructor' || key === 'prototype') return;
if (current[key] == null) current[key] = ...;
current = current[key];
...
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

- The guard line (`key === '__proto__' || ...`, lines 50-52) is the intended defense; it is safe only for primitive string segments.
- `current = current[key]` (lines 53-57) is where a non-primitive segment is coerced into a forbidden key — this is the traversal that escapes the response object.
- `current[finalKey] = ...` (lines 59-64) is the sink: the write that lands on `Object.prototype`.
- The final-segment check at lines 60-62 repeats the same strict-equality pattern and has the same weakness.

## Reproduction

**Verified — reproduced dynamically, not only by inspection.** Three independent reproductions were run:

1. **Source level.** `packages/utils/src/{mergeIncrementalResult,mergeDeep,helpers}.ts` were copied from `master` unchanged except for retargeting relative `.js` import specifiers to `.ts`, then run under `node --experimental-strip-types --test`. 5/5 tests pass, including a control proving that the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment **is** blocked, while the payload `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":{"pwned":true}}` sets `Object.prototype.polluted = {pwned: true}` and leaves the `executionResult` as `{"data":{}}`. The `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.
2. **Published artifacts.** The same attacks were run against the real npm dist builds: 10.10.0 = 0/5 attacks succeed (still uses `dset`, which blocks it); 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0 and 12.0.1 = 5/5 attacks succeed. This differential confirms the affected range and that `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` introduced the issue; that commit is still the last one touching the file on `master`, so HEAD (`ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`) is unfixed.
3. **Real call site over the network.** A local HTTP server returned a spec-shaped `multipart/mixed` `@defer` response whose deferred patches carry `path: [["__proto__"],"isAdmin"]`. The client only `JSON.parse()`d the chunks and called the public `mergeIncrementalResult()`. Afterwards `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` contains `isAdmin` and `ownerEmail`, `({}).isAdmin === true`, and a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a fresh `{}` returns `true`.

Minimal standalone reproduction:

```ts
import { mergeIncrementalResult } from '@graphql-tools/utils';

const executionResult = { data: {} };
const incrementalResult = JSON.parse('{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}');
mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult });
console.log(({} as any).polluted); // expected vulnerable output: yes
delete (Object.prototype as any).polluted;
```

Steps: run the above under Node against the built `@graphql-tools/utils` package, then inspect a freshly created object after the merge.

- **Expected:** the helper rejects the malformed path; `({} as any).polluted` remains `undefined` and no property is added to `Object.prototype`.
- **Actual:** the write lands on `Object.prototype`; `({} as any).polluted` is `"yes"` on a fresh object, while `executionResult` is left as `{"data":{}}`.

## Suggested remediation

Validate the type of every path segment before it is used for property access, so that only primitive string/number keys ever reach bracket access — and compare against the forbidden names only after that validation.

```ts
function isSafeKey(key: unknown): key is string | number {
  if (typeof key !== 'string' && typeof key !== 'number') return false;
  return key !== '__proto__' && key !== 'constructor' && key !== 'prototype';
}

// walking segment
const key = keyPath[i];
if (!isSafeKey(key)) return;
if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, key) || current[key] == null) {
  current[key] = ...;
}
current = current[key];

// final segment
if (!isSafeKey(finalKey)) return;
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

A stronger variant, if it fits the project's style: build intermediate containers with `Object.create(null)` and use own-property access (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`) throughout the walk, so an inherited property can never be resolved or written even if a future guard is missed.

Notes:

- The final-segment check (lines 60-62) needs the same treatment as the walking check (lines 50-52); patching only one leaves the other reachable.
- All three branches that reach this sink — `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and the recursive `incremental[]` handling — are affected by the same helper and are fixed together by validating in `setObjectKeyPath`.
- Nothing outside this helper appears to need changing: 10.10.0 and earlier, which delegated to `dset`, were not exploitable by any of the tested payloads, so the regression is confined to the hand-rolled traversal added in `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713`.
- Whether a released fix or backport policy is wanted for the 10.x and 11.x lines is the maintainers' call; no fix, advisory, or upstream issue currently exists for this.

Suggested regression test alongside the existing tests for `mergeIncrementalResult` (exact spec file path: **unknown** — not identified in this review): assert that merging `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}` leaves `({} as any).polluted` `undefined` and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` unchanged, with a paired control asserting the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment is still rejected, and equivalents for an object-valued segment (e.g. `{"toString":() => "__proto__"}`-style coercion) and for the `items`/`incremental[]` branches.

## Resolution

Fixed in `@graphql-tools/utils@12.0.2`, which is published on npm. `setObjectKeyPath` rejects a path unless every segment is a primitive string or number, and still blocks `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype`. Upgrade to `>=12.0.2`.

summary: DOMPurify SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES bypass: split template expressions survive in attached shadow root content on DOM output modes
description:
## Summary

When DOMPurify is configured with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true` together with a DOM-returning mode (`RETURN_DOM: true`, `RETURN_DOM_FRAGMENT: true`, or `IN_PLACE: true`), template expressions such as `{{...}}`, `${...}`, and `<%...%>` survive sanitization inside the text content of an attached shadow root. The post-walk safety net `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:1717`) was extended to recurse into `<template>.content`, but it never recurses into attached shadow roots. An attacker who can supply a DOM node carrying a shadow root (the `IN_PLACE` and shadow-aware `RETURN_DOM` surfaces) can split an expression across text nodes separated by disallowed elements; after those elements are removed the fragments become adjacent and serialize into a complete expression that a downstream template engine will evaluate.

## Root Cause

`SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` neutralizes template expressions through two mechanisms: a per-text-node strip during the main walk (`_stripTemplateExpressions`, applied in `_sanitizeElements` at `src/purify.ts:2246`), and a final post-walk pass (`_scrubTemplateExpressions`, `src/purify.ts:1717`) that normalizes adjacent text nodes and re-strips expressions that only form after merging. The per-node strip cannot catch an expression that is split into individual fragments, because each fragment fails the delimiter regexes. The post-walk pass is the only mechanism that would catch the merged form, but it is structurally unable to reach shadow root content.

```text
_scrubTemplateExpressions (src/purify.ts:1717-1751):
  - node.normalize() at line 1718 does not merge text nodes inside shadow roots (DOM spec).
  - NodeIterator at lines 1723-1731 does not descend into shadow trees (DOM spec).
  - Explicit recursion at lines 1743-1750 enters <template>.content only, via
    querySelectorAll('template'); there is no equivalent recursion into attached
    shadow roots.
Shadow roots are sanitized earlier by _sanitizeShadowDOM (src/purify.ts:2710), which
applies the per-node strip but never performs the post-walk normalize-and-rescrub.
```

Shadow root text nodes are therefore sanitized only per-node and never re-examined as a merged unit.

## Impact

An attacker who controls DOM-node input containing an attached shadow root can inject template expressions that survive sanitization and are later evaluated by the application's template engine. In client-side contexts this yields cross-site scripting; in a server-side template context it can escalate to template injection. Exploitation requires non-default application configuration: the application must enable `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` and a DOM-returning mode, pass a DOM node that already has an attached shadow root, and feed the sanitized shadow root content into a template evaluator. The shadow root does not have to be built programmatically with `attachShadow`: in engines that support declarative shadow DOM, attacker-supplied markup containing `<template shadowrootmode="open">` parsed through `setHTMLUnsafe` or `Document.parseHTMLUnsafe` produces the same attached shadow root, so a plain HTML string reaches the gap once the application is configured this way. Demonstrated capability is injection of a complete, attacker-chosen expression into post-sanitization shadow root content; the resulting script execution and any confidentiality or integrity consequence depend on the downstream engine's evaluation context.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Preconditions:
  - DOMPurify built from the affected source (dist/purify.js or an ESM/CJS bundle).
  - A browser (or DOM implementation) with shadow DOM support.
  - Application constructs a DOM node with an attached shadow root before sanitizing,
    and later evaluates the shadow root's text content as a template.
```

Build a host element whose shadow root holds a template expression split across text nodes separated by disallowed elements, then sanitize in place with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`:

```javascript
const host = document.createElement('div');
const root = host.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });

// Split "${alert(document.domain)}" so no single fragment matches a regex.
// <object> is not in the default ALLOWED_TAGS and is removed during sanitization,
// leaving the surrounding text-node siblings adjacent.
root.appendChild(document.createTextNode('$'));
root.appendChild(document.createElement('object'));
root.appendChild(document.createTextNode('{alert(document.domain)}'));

DOMPurify.sanitize(host, { IN_PLACE: true, SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true });

// After the disallowed element is removed, the fragments are adjacent and survive.
host.shadowRoot.normalize();
console.log(host.shadowRoot.textContent);
```

```text
${alert(document.domain)}
```

A downstream template evaluator reading `shadowRoot.textContent` (for example `new Function('return `' + content + '`')()` or any `${...}`/`{{...}}` engine) then evaluates the fully formed expression.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The application calls `DOMPurify.sanitize(node, cfg)` (`src/purify.ts:2854`) with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true` and `IN_PLACE: true` (or a shadow-aware `RETURN_DOM`), passing a DOM node that already carries an attached shadow root.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the shadow root's text nodes and the disallowed separator elements between them; each fragment (`$`, `{alert(document.domain)}`) is a valid, individually benign text node.
3. **Path:** `_sanitizeAttachedShadowRoots` (`src/purify.ts:2977`) feeds the shadow root into `_sanitizeShadowDOM` (`src/purify.ts:2710`), which strips expressions per text node (`src/purify.ts:2246`) and removes the disallowed separator elements, leaving the fragments adjacent.
4. **Guard:** The post-walk safety net `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:3131-3132`) is the only pass that would catch the merged expression, but it never recurses into shadow roots (`src/purify.ts:1717-1751` recurses into `<template>.content` only).
5. **Primitive:** The adjacent fragments serialize as a single concatenated string on `shadowRoot.textContent` / `shadowRoot.innerHTML`, reconstituting the complete expression.
6. **Result:** A downstream template engine evaluates the attacker-chosen expression, achieving script execution (or template injection) in the engine's context.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protection is `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`, specifically the post-walk pass that defends against expressions that only form after adjacent text nodes merge. That defense was previously extended to `<template>.content` under CVE-2026-65900 (GHSA-gvmj-g25r-r7wr) by adding `querySelectorAll('template')` recursion at `src/purify.ts:1743-1750`. The strongest challenge is whether any code path performs the equivalent merge-and-rescrub inside shadow roots. Enumerating every call site of `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:1717`, `1747`, `3132`, `3141`) shows none receive a shadow root, and `_sanitizeShadowDOM` (`src/purify.ts:2710`) never calls `_scrubTemplateExpressions` or `normalize()`. The per-node strip cannot compensate: `MUSTACHE_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:3`) requires `{{` or `}}`, `TMPLIT_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:5`) requires `${`, and `ERB_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:4`) requires `<%` or `%>`, none of which appear in a single-character fragment. The CVE-2026-65900 regression tests exercise `<template>.content` only; no test covers shadow root content under `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`. The gap is therefore an unfixed case on a distinct remediation boundary (shadow roots) rather than a bypass of the delivered template-content fix.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `npm`
- **Package:** `dompurify`
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 3.4.4, <= 3.4.16`
- **Latest release checked:** `3.4.16` ([npm registry](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dompurify/v/3.4.16))
- **Fix status:** not fixed

The lower bound 3.4.4 is the release that introduced both the attached-shadow-root sanitization pass and the `_scrubTemplateExpressions` safety net; releases 3.4.4 through 3.4.7 carry the safety net with no content-container recursion, and 3.4.8 onward add `<template>.content` recursion but still omit shadow root recursion. No published release and no current development revision contains a shadow-root fix.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce the same post-walk normalize-and-rescrub invariant on attached shadow roots that already applies to `<template>.content`. After `_sanitizeShadowDOM` finishes walking a shadow root, run `_scrubTemplateExpressions` over that shadow root so adjacent text nodes created by element removal are merged and re-stripped; alternatively, have `_scrubTemplateExpressions` discover and recurse into attached shadow roots as it does for template content. The fix must cover nested shadow roots and shadow roots inside `<template>.content`, and it must handle all three expression dialects, since any disallowed element can serve as the separator that produces adjacent fragments.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

summary: next.js cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions
description:
### Impact

With Cache Components enabled (`cacheComponents: true`), a `'use cache'` function that calls another `'use cache'` function that reads a root param can be keyed incorrectly when the inner call is served from an existing entry: the enclosing function's cache key then omits that root param. The enclosing entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value — whether the page is prerendered at build time or at runtime, or rendered dynamically. Shared cache headers let downstream caches redistribute the content further. 

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds. Apps should upgrade to the patched version as soon as possible.

summary: Sentry-Javascript: Middleware Bypass when using Tunnel route
description:
### Impact

The `tunnelRoute` option makes the SDK send browser events to a path on your own Next.js server (for example `/monitoring`), where a rewrite forwards them to Sentry to prevent ad blockers from blocking them. To keep those envelope requests from being rejected by your middleware, the SDK skips middleware for them.

The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite. The rewrite only serves requests to the tunnel path itself with the `o` and `p` parameters set. The skip applied to anything under the tunnel path. Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

Skipping middleware does not grant the request any privileges. Routes that check the session server-side are still protected.

You are affected only if **all** of the following are true:

1. `tunnelRoute` is set (a string path or `true`),
2. your app is built with **webpack** (Turbopack builds are not affected),
3. some route of your application resolves under the tunnel path. That could be a direct collision (`/monitoring/foo` with `tunnelRoute: '/monitoring'`) or a dynamic segment at the route root (`app/[locale]/…`), which matches any first path segment, and
4. your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes.

Sentry's own services, and the data in your Sentry organization, are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in [9.47.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/9.47.2), [10.75.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/10.75.2) and [11.0.0-rc.1](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/11.0.0-rc.1). The skip now matches only the requests the tunnel rewrite actually serves. No configuration change is needed.

### Workarounds

- Set `tunnelRoute` to a path no route of yours can resolve under, or remove the option.
- Build with Turbopack (default for `next build` from Next.js 16).
- Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

summary: stream-json: FlexAssembler string/RegExp path filters join the full key stack per container start, giving O(depth^2) CPU denial of service
description:
## Summary

`FlexAssembler`, the custom-container assembler shipped in the `stream-json` package (`src/core/utils/flex-assembler.js`, re-exported at `stream-json/utils/flex-assembler.js` and `stream-json/web/utils/flex-assembler.js`), compiles a string or RegExp path `filter` into a matcher that runs `keyStack.join(separator)` on every container start. Because the key stack grows one entry per open object or array with no depth bound, a JSON document nested to depth D drives D container-start tokens that each perform an O(D) join, for O(D^2) total CPU on the single-threaded event loop. An unauthenticated party who can supply JSON bytes to a pipeline that uses a `FlexAssembler` with a string or RegExp rule filter can stall the process with a small input: roughly 96 KB (depth 16000) blocks the event loop for over a second, and the cost grows quadratically.

## Root Cause

`FlexAssembler` reconstructs JavaScript values from the parser token stream and supports custom containers selected by path-matching rules. When a rule `filter` is a string or RegExp, `compileFilter` returns a matcher that computes the joined path from the full key stack before making any match decision. That join is O(current depth), and it is invoked unconditionally for every rule on every container start. The key stack that feeds the join has no depth cap. The package does have a depth guard (`maxDepth`), but it exists only in the unrelated filter base state machine and never executes on the `FlexAssembler` code path, so nested input is unbounded here.

```text
src/core/utils/flex-assembler.js
  compileFilter (lines 5-21): string branch computes `path.join(separator)` (line 10)
    before the `=== filter || startsWith(...)` comparison; RegExp branch computes
    `filter.test(path.join(separator))` (line 17). The join runs first, unconditionally.
  FlexAssembler._matchRule (lines 160-166): calls `rule.filter(this.keyStack)` for every
    rule; invoked from startObject (line 184) and startArray (line 197) on every
    container start.
  FlexAssembler._pushState (lines 168-176): pushes one entry onto `keyStack` per open
    container with no depth bound.
```

## Impact

An attacker who can deliver JSON to a pipeline whose `FlexAssembler` is configured with a string or RegExp rule filter (a documented, tested, first-class option: `Filter = string | RegExp | FilterFunction`) can cause quadratic CPU consumption. The join runs regardless of whether the rule ultimately matches, so no attacker knowledge of the schema is required beyond nesting depth, which the attacker fully controls. The demonstrated capability is an availability impact: a small crafted document blocks the Node.js event loop, stalling all concurrent work on the process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. A consumer that uses only a function filter or no rules is not affected, which narrows the vulnerable population but does not raise attack complexity once such a configuration is in use.

## Proof of Concept

`Node.js and the published stream-json@3.6.0 package. Drive a FlexAssembler configured with a string rule filter, comparing against a function filter as a negative control.`

1. Install `stream-json@3.6.0`.
2. Construct a deeply nested object token stream (or equivalently parse a document like `'{"k":'` repeated D times, a `1`, then `'}'` repeated D times, through `parser`/`parserStream`).
3. Feed it to a `FlexAssembler` whose `objectRules` contains a rule with a string `filter`.
4. Observe wall-clock time scaling as roughly 4x per doubling of D (quadratic), while a function-filter configuration stays flat.

```js
import FlexAssembler from 'stream-json/utils/flex-assembler.js';

function run(filter, D) {
  const asm = new FlexAssembler(filter ? {objectRules: [{filter, create: () => ({})}]} : undefined);
  const t = performance.now();
  asm.startObject();
  for (let i = 0; i < D; i++) { asm.keyValue('k'); asm.startObject(); }
  return performance.now() - t;
}

for (const D of [4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]) console.log('string', D, run('k', D).toFixed(1), 'ms');
for (const D of [4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]) console.log('function(control)', D, run(p => p.length > 0, D).toFixed(1), 'ms');
```

```text
string filter (path.join per token):     function filter (negative control, no join):
  D=4000     91.9 ms                        D=4000     1.6 ms
  D=8000    341.9 ms                        D=8000     0.9 ms
  D=16000  1359.2 ms  (~4x per doubling)    D=16000    1.7 ms   (flat)
  D=32000  5430.0 ms  (= O(D^2))            D=32000    2.6 ms
```

End to end through a real `parserStream`, roughly 96 KB (depth 16000) of attacker-supplied JSON stalls the event loop for over 1.3 seconds.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The attacker supplies JSON bytes to a service pipeline that assembles values with a `FlexAssembler` configured with a string or RegExp rule filter; `FlexAssembler` is a documented submodule of the published package on both the Node and Web Streams surfaces.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the JSON bytes and therefore the nesting depth D, which directly controls the key stack length.
3. **Path:** Each `{` or `[` emits `startObject`/`startArray`, which push onto `keyStack` and call `_matchRule`, which calls the compiled filter with the current key stack.
4. **Guard:** There is no depth or size cap on this path; the only `maxDepth` guard in the package lives in the filter base state machine and never runs in `FlexAssembler`.
5. **Primitive:** For each of the D container starts, the compiled string/RegExp filter runs an O(D) `join` before any match decision, for O(D^2) total CPU.
6. **Result:** The single-threaded event loop stalls, denying service to all concurrent work on the process; a small input scales quadratically to sustained unavailability.

## Bypass Evidence

This is a novel finding on a code path that no prior fix protects, so there is no guard to bypass on the `FlexAssembler` path. The relevant prior fix is the `maxDepth` cap published as part of the remediation for CVE-2026-71429 (GHSA-528h-pc64-c93x), which addressed the analogous O(depth^2) behavior in the `pick`/`ignore`/`filter`/`replace` filters. That fix was placed only in `src/core/filters/filter-base.js`; `src/core/utils/flex-assembler.js` neither imports nor invokes it, so the guard never executes here. A search for `maxDepth` across `src/` returns only the filter base file and its type declaration, and `flex-assembler.js` imports only `{none}` from `stream-chain/core`. Attempts to refute the finding all failed: the join was confirmed to run unconditionally before the match comparison in both the string and RegExp branches; a function-filter negative control stayed flat while the string filter scaled at 4x per doubling, isolating the join as the quadratic cause; and the behavior was reproduced both by driving `FlexAssembler` directly and end to end through a real parser pipeline. This is not the same issue as the JSONC comment re-scan advisory (GHSA-hqr4-qq8f-hg3x) or the Assembler prototype pollution advisory (GHSA-mjw6-4jj6-33hc), which involve different components, mechanisms, and impact classes.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: stream-json`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 2.0.0, <= 3.6.0`
- `Latest release checked: 3.6.0 (npm registry latest)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

`FlexAssembler` was introduced in 2.0.0; the 1.x line has no such component. The vulnerable `compileFilter` join branches, the uncapped key stack, and the absence of any depth guard are present and effectively identical across the 2.0.0 through 3.6.0 releases, including the current registry `latest` (3.6.0). No fixed release exists: the depth cap shipped for the related filter issue does not touch `FlexAssembler`, so every release in the range is affected and a future release remains affected until a `FlexAssembler`-side bound ships.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a nesting depth bound on the `FlexAssembler` assembly path, mirroring the `maxDepth` guard already used by the filter base state machine, so that pathologically deep input is rejected before it drives quadratic work. Alternatively, or in addition, eliminate the per-container full-stack `join` in `compileFilter` by maintaining the joined path incrementally (append the new segment on push, truncate on pop) or by comparing the key stack against the filter with a prefix walk that is O(1) amortized per container start rather than O(depth). Any fix must cover both the string and RegExp filter branches and both the object and array rule paths, on both the Node and Web Streams surfaces. As an interim mitigation without a code change, consumers can use function filters (which do not perform the join) or impose an upstream input size or depth limit before the parser.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

---

# Maintainer note on scope

The attack vector is local — stream-json's documented input is data the user owns (dumps, exports, logs, configuration you wrote); it is not designed for JSON from the open internet, and the docs say so. The crafted document reaches the vulnerable component as a buffer, so `AV:L` gives 6.2, the same vector and score as GHSA-528h-pc64-c93x and GHSA-hqr4-qq8f-hg3x. `FlexAssembler` now takes a `maxDepth` option, default `1024`, which throws a `RangeError` before any rule is matched; `Infinity` opts out, and once rules are configured the cap covers containers of both kinds, because a rule's path state is kept at every level whatever kind it matches. A follow-up went past what the advisory needed and removed the per-check join entirely — a string filter keeps prefix-match state per level, a RegExp an accumulated path, a function filter the parts array it already received — so deeply nested input is linear now rather than merely capped.
