summary: ApostropheCMS: Authenticated projection-exclusion prototype-member deletion in @apostrophecms/db-connect causes process-wide denial of service
description:
## Summary

`@apostrophecms/db-connect` ships an in-memory MongoDB emulation used by its SQLite, PostgreSQL, and multipostgres adapters. Its `unsetNestedField` helper walks an attacker-controlled dotted field path with no segment validation and calls `delete` on the resolved property. A low-privileged authenticated user (any role holding `view-draft`, which every editor and contributor has; reduced to any logged-in user when `guestApiAccess` is enabled) can send a piece-type REST GET request whose `project` query builder contains an exclusion key such as `constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty`. On a SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter this key reaches `unsetNestedField`, which resolves `Object.prototype` and deletes a shared runtime method. Because that method is shared across the whole Node process, the deletion breaks request handling for every tenant and user until the process is restarted, giving a single request a persistent denial of service.

## Root Cause

The projection query builder laundens only projection values, never projection keys, so an arbitrary dotted key survives to the database layer. On the SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters an exclusion projection is applied in JavaScript by `applyProjection`, which for each excluded field calls `unsetNestedField(result, field)`. `unsetNestedField` splits the field on `.` and walks the resulting segments with no guard: unlike its sibling `setNestedField`, it does not even block a literal `__proto__`, and neither helper blocks `constructor` or `prototype`. Because the working object is a plain object produced by `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))`, its `constructor` resolves to the global `Object`, so a path of `constructor.prototype.<member>` reaches the shared `Object.prototype` and deletes a core, configurable method. The violated invariant is that untrusted input must never be able to traverse into and mutate shared prototype objects.

```text
Affected functions (repository-relative paths):
- unsetNestedField  packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:119-129  (no segment guard; delete on resolved property)
- applyProjection   packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:164-216  (exclusion branch calls unsetNestedField per excluded key)
Reachability driver (consumer on a SQL adapter):
- project.launder / project.finalize  packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:2003-2103
- getRestQuery                        packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1139-1157
- SQLite adapter applyProjection call packages/db-connect/adapters/sqlite.js:906,980
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: an authenticated account holding `view-draft` (every editing role; any logged-in user when `guestApiAccess: true`), and a consumer configured to use a SQLite, PostgreSQL, or multipostgres adapter. The default `mongodb` adapter hands the projection to the real MongoDB driver and is not affected. With those conditions, a single crafted GET request deletes an attacker-chosen shared prototype method (for example `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`, `toString`, or an `Array.prototype` member). The demonstrated capability is a persistent, process-wide denial of service: after the deletion, ordinary calls such as `obj.hasOwnProperty(...)` throw across Apostrophe, its dependencies, and the database driver, so the affected Node process cannot service requests for any user until it is restarted. The attacker chooses which member to remove, and the corruption of shared runtime state persists for the life of the process.

## Proof of Concept

`The finding was reproduced by executing the shipped helper directly against the published db-connect source; a live consumer requires a SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter, an authenticated view-draft session, and at least one matching document.`

1. Authenticate as any user with `view-draft` on a site whose database adapter is `sqlite`, `postgres`, or `multipostgres`.
2. Issue a piece-type REST read with an exclusion projection whose key targets a shared prototype method.
3. Observe that subsequent requests fail process-wide because the shared method was deleted.

```text
GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/article?project[constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty]=0
Cookie: <authenticated view-draft session>
```

```text
safe        benign exclusion {title:0} leaves Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty intact
VULNERABLE  exclusion projection deleted Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty (callableBefore=true, brokeEveryObject=true)
VULNERABLE  exclusion projection deleted an arbitrary Object.prototype method (__pocMarker)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An authenticated `view-draft` user calls the piece-type REST GET endpoint `GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/<piece-type>`, which is reachable by any editing role.
2. **Control:** The query string `project[constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty]=0` is parsed by `qs` (with `allowDots` off) into a single own key with literal dots, `{ 'constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty': '0' }`.
3. **Path:** `getRestQuery` applies the query builders first; `project.launder` copies the key verbatim and coerces only the value to `false`; `project.finalize` skips the falsy value with `if (!val) continue` and preserves the key; the cursor stores it as the projection.
4. **Guard:** The `publicApiProjection` override that would discard the attacker projection runs only when `canAccessApi(req)` is false, so it is skipped for the authenticated caller; no key allowlist, segment check, or prototype guard exists anywhere on the path.
5. **Primitive:** On the SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter, `applyProjection` takes the exclusion branch and calls `unsetNestedField(result, 'constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty')`, which resolves `Object.prototype` and executes `delete Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`.
6. **Result:** A shared prototype method is removed for the entire Node process, so request handling throws for all users and tenants until restart.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protections were examined individually and none blocks this path. The projection `launder` (packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:2003-2011) laundens values only and retains arbitrary keys. The `publicApiProjection` permission override (packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1142-1156) is gated on `!canAccessApi(req)` and is therefore not taken for an authenticated `view-draft` caller. The `finalize` per-key loop (doc-type/index.js:2062-2069) short-circuits on the falsy exclusion value before it ever inspects the key. Most importantly, `unsetNestedField` (packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:119-129) has no segment guard at all: its sibling `setNestedField` blocks a literal `__proto__` but neither helper blocks `constructor` or `prototype`, and the `constructor.prototype.<member>` path bypasses even that partial `__proto__` check. Attempts to disprove the finding all failed: routing the value to the inclusion branch (which uses `setNestedField`) does not occur because the value is falsy; the working object is a plain object from `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))` so its `constructor` is the global `Object`; and `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` is configurable, so the delete succeeds. The seed prototype-pollution fix added a `{__proto__, constructor, prototype}` segment guard, but only in `apos.util.set`/`get` in the separate `apostrophe` package; the db-connect helpers were never hardened.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: @apostrophecms/db-connect`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 1.0.0, <= 1.0.2`
- `Latest release checked: 1.0.2 (npm registry)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The unguarded `unsetNestedField` and the exclusion-branch `applyProjection` call are byte-identical across the published stable releases 1.0.0, 1.0.1, and 1.0.2, and the SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters invoke `applyProjection` per returned document in all of them. No published release fixes the issue. The prerelease line (1.0.0-alpha.1, 1.0.0-alpha.2, 1.0.2-alpha.0) ships the same code but is outside the supported stable channel. Reachability requires a consumer on a SQLite, PostgreSQL, or multipostgres adapter; the default `mongodb` adapter delegates the projection to the real MongoDB driver and is not affected. The `apostrophe` package, which drives reachability, declares `@apostrophecms/db-connect@^1.0.1`, resolving to the affected 1.0.2.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce that untrusted field paths can never traverse into shared prototype objects. Both `unsetNestedField` and `setNestedField` in `packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js` should reject any path whose segments include `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`, mirroring the `unsafePathSegments` guard already used in the `apostrophe` package's `apos.util.set`/`get`; equivalently, the helpers can traverse own-properties only (for example using `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` checks captured before use, or `Map`-based access) so that resolution cannot reach prototype objects. Because `applyProjection` is the reachable gate, adding the guard at the helper level protects every adapter path at once. As an interim mitigation without a code change, deployments can run on the default `mongodb` adapter (which is not affected) or restrict authenticated API access so that only fully trusted roles can reach the piece-type REST endpoints.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

summary: @angular/router: Denial of Service via RouterLink Query Parameter Retention in Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
description:
A denial of service (DoS) vulnerability was identified in `@angular/router` when Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is enabled on Node.js (V8) and `RouterLink` directives are rendered with `queryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'`, configured either per link or globally via `defaultQueryParamsHandling`.

Starting in v21.2.0 ([angular/angular#66181](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/66181)), `RouterLink` internals were refactored to use signals, introducing a computed signal (`_urlTree`) that cached the returned `UrlTree` instance on the directive. Because each rendered link maintains an active `RouterLink` instance for the entire duration of the request lifecycle, the computed signal permanently pinned the `UrlTree` and its associated query parameter dictionary in the heap until the SSR response completed.

When query parameter handling is set to `'merge'` or `'preserve'`, each link copies the incoming request's query parameters into its own `UrlTree`. During SSR, memory consumption scales multiplicatively:

$$\text{Heap Retention} \approx (\text{Number of affected links}) \times (\text{Size of parsed query parameter map})$$

Because parsed JavaScript objects and property dictionaries require substantially more heap space than the raw query string—particularly when property names trigger dense array allocations under V8 property-storage heuristics—an attacker can supply oversized query strings to amplify heap consumption by orders of magnitude per in-flight request.

### Impact

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust the Node.js old-space heap with modest concurrent request volume, terminating the SSR worker with an unrecoverable JavaScript heap out of memory fatal crash.

* **Numeric Names Not Required:** Numeric query parameter names trigger larger V8 property-storage allocations (~558 KB per parsed dictionary in tests vs. ~197 KB for non-numeric equivalents), lowering the concurrency threshold needed for a crash. However, non-numeric query parameters also produce significant heap amplification and can exhaust worker memory with proportionally higher concurrency.
* **Client-side SPAs Unaffected:** Pure client-side Angular applications (Single Page Applications without SSR) are not vulnerable, as local browser memory consumption does not cross a security boundary.

### Attack Preconditions & Vulnerable Configurations

An application is affected only if all of the following conditions are met:

1. **SSR Enabled:** The application runs in a Server-Side Rendering environment powered by Node.js / V8.
2. **Merged or Preserved Query Parameters:** `RouterLink` elements rendered during SSR use `queryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'`, either bound explicitly on links or configured application-wide via `withRouterConfig({ defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge' })`.
3. **Upstream Proxy Forwards Long Request Lines:** Reverse proxies or load balancers (e.g., Nginx, AWS ALB, Cloudflare) forward long query strings to the Node.js application rather than rejecting them at the edge. (For example, Nginx's default 8 KB `large_client_header_buffers` limit rejects 16 KB request lines unless explicitly increased).
4. **Overlapping Renders:** Because retained memory is freed once each request completes, multiple concurrent requests must be processed simultaneously in the same Node.js worker instance (such as pages awaiting asynchronous data fetching, route resolvers, or external API calls during SSR).

### Exploit Payload Example

An attacker issues concurrent HTTP requests containing dense query parameters to an SSR page that renders multiple merged links:

```http
GET /products?0&17&34&51&68&85&...&48042 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
```

### Patches

The issue is resolved by removing persistent `UrlTree` retention from `RouterLink` ([angular/angular#70953](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/70953)). `RouterLink` now tracks route dependencies directly in `reactiveHref` and discards intermediate `UrlTree` instances immediately after computing the serialized href string. The `urlTree` getter and click handlers compute `UrlTree` instances on demand.

As a result, intermediate query parameter maps are short-lived allocations collected during young-generation GC scavenges rather than remaining pinned in the heap for the lifetime of the request, restoring the memory profile of Angular 21.1 and earlier.

Patched versions:
* `22.2.1`
* `21.2.25`

Versions prior to 21.2.0 (including Angular 20.x LTS and 21.1.x) do not retain `UrlTree` instances in `RouterLink` and are not vulnerable to this issue.

### Workarounds & Mitigations

If you cannot immediately upgrade to a patched version, apply one or more of the following mitigations:

1. **Avoid 'merge' and 'preserve' on Server-Rendered Links:**
   Remove `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` (or `'preserve'`) from global configuration. Explicitly bind only the specific query parameters each link requires (e.g., `[queryParams]="{ filter: filter() }"`). Even on patched versions, this practice prevents unnecessary request-derived parameter propagation into generated DOM markup.

2. **Limit Query String Length at Reverse Proxy or Middleware:**
   Configure your edge proxy, web application firewall (WAF), or reverse proxy to reject requests with excessively long query strings (e.g., exceeding 2,048 bytes).

   Alternatively, reject oversized query strings in Node.js before Angular SSR handles the request:
   ```ts
   // server.ts (before Angular SSR handler)
   app.use((req, res, next) => {
     const queryIndex = req.url.indexOf('?');
     if (queryIndex !== -1 && req.url.length - queryIndex > 2048) {
       res.status(414).send('URI Too Long');
       return;
     }
     next();
   });
   ```

3. **Increase Node.js Old Space:**
   Increasing `--max-old-space-size` (e.g., to 2048 MB or 4096 MB) increases the memory headroom and the concurrency threshold required to exhaust memory, though it does not fully eliminate vulnerability under sustained traffic.

summary: Hono: `serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time, leading to bypass of middleware on static paths
description:
### Summary

`serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time after Hono has already decoded it for routing. A crafted request can be routed as one path and served as another, so middleware mounted on a static prefix does not run for a file under that prefix.

### Details

Hono decodes the request path once before routing. `serveStatic` decoded it again before resolving the file. With a malformed percent-encoded sequence, the first decode leaves part of the path encoded, the router matches the encoded form, and the second decode resolves the real directory. The file is still resolved inside the configured root; this is not a traversal outside it.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker may reach static files without the middleware on their prefix running, for example an authentication check. This affects applications that mount middleware on part of the directory served by `serveStatic`. Applications that serve only public files are not affected.

summary: @angular/platform-server: Open Redirect via Protocol-Relative URLs in Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
description:
An open redirect vulnerability was identified in `@angular/platform-server` when Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is enabled.

When Angular SSR renders an incoming request, URL resolution and platform navigation are managed by `ServerPlatformLocation` using `resolveUrl` (or `parseUrl` in v20). While `resolveUrl` rejected protocol-relative URLs whose raw string directly started with `//`, this check ran *prior* to WHATWG URL normalization.

When a request URL includes a popping dot-segment followed by multiple slashes (such as `/.//evil.test` or serialized from router route shapes like `/.;/(//evil.test)`), the input bypassed the initial `urlStr.startsWith('//')` check. Subsequent WHATWG URL parsing resolved the dot-segments and resulted in a `pathname` starting with `//` (`//evil.test`).

Consequently, `ServerPlatformLocation` stored `pathname = '//evil.test'`. When `@angular/ssr` detected a mismatch between the rendered URL and the router's final location state, it emitted the unnormalized pathname into the HTTP `Location` response header, producing an HTTP 302 redirect with `Location: //evil.test`, which browsers resolve as a protocol-relative navigation off-origin.

### Impact

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to craft URLs that trick Angular SSR into redirecting users to an arbitrary external domain.

* **Bypasses Application-Level Guards:** Common application-level validation routines (such as checking `!returnUrl.startsWith('//')` before invoking `router.navigateByUrl`) accept `/.//evil.test` or `/.;/(//evil.test)` as a safe relative path, allowing attackers to bypass redirect allowlists.
* **Client-side SPAs Unaffected:** Pure client-side Angular applications (Single Page Applications without SSR) are **not** vulnerable, as `ServerPlatformLocation` is only utilized in server-side execution environments.

### Attack Preconditions & Vulnerable Configurations

An application is affected if the following conditions are met:

* **SSR Enabled:** The application runs in a Server-Side Rendering environment using `@angular/platform-server` and `@angular/ssr`.
* **Parameter Route Shapes:** The router contains parameter routes with wildcard or child segments (e.g. `/:tenant` matching `.` and serializing secondary outlet groups `(//evil.test)` to `/.//evil.test`), or passes user-provided navigation targets (e.g. `returnUrl`).
* **Reverse Proxy Passthrough:** Upstream reverse proxies (Nginx, Cloudflare, ALB) pass semicolons (`;`) or dot-segments without stripping or normalizing them.

#### Exploit Payload Example

An attacker sends a request targeting a route with parameters and child segments:

```http
GET /.;/(//evil.test) HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
```

**Response:**
```http
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: //evil.test
```

The client browser resolves `//evil.test` protocol-relatively and redirects the user away from `example.com` to `evil.test`.

### Patches

The issue is resolved by updating `resolveUrl` (and `parseUrl` in v20) in `@angular/platform-server` to verify that the normalized URL pathname does not start with `//` when `allowProtocolRelative` is `false`.

* `22.2.1`
* `21.2.25`
* `20.3.33`

### Workarounds & Mitigations

If you cannot immediately upgrade to a patched version, apply one of the following mitigations at your edge reverse proxy or WAF:

1. **Reject Paths with Dot-Segments Followed by Slashes:**
   Configure your reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx, Cloudflare, AWS WAF) to block requests containing `/.//`, `/..//`, or `/.;/`:
   ```nginx
   # Nginx example: reject suspicious path normalization sequences
   if ($request_uri ~* "(\n/\.\/|\/\.\;)") {
       return 400;
   }
   ```
2. **Sanitize Redirect Headers:**
   Ensure edge proxies or API gateways rewrite or disallow protocol-relative (`//`) `Location` response headers originating from the SSR upstream.

summary: markdown-it: Quadratic complexity in smartquotes with unmatched closing quotes
description:
### Impact

When `typographer: true` is enabled, specially crafted Markdown can cause quadratic processing time in the smartquotes rule, potentially leading to denial of service in applications processing untrusted input.

Many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes cause repeated scans of the entire opener stack. The same issue occurs with the quote types reversed.

The default configuration (`typographer: false`) is not affected, but this option is enabled with high probability.

### Reproduction

```js
import MarkdownIt from 'markdown-it'
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const md = new MarkdownIt({ typographer: true })

for (const k of [2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]) {
  const input = '"a '.repeat(k) + "b' ".repeat(k)
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(input)
  console.log(input.length, (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1), 'ms')
}
```

Result:

|input size|time|
|-|-|
|12000|18ms|
|24000|47ms|
|48000|115ms|
|96000|428ms|
|192000|1586ms|

### Patches

Fixed in **15.0.2** and **14.3.2**.

### Workarounds

Disable typography with `typographer: false`, or disable only the smartquotes rule:

```js
md.disable('smartquotes')
```

summary: ckan-mcp-server: DataStore Table UI resource does not validate postMessage origin (in) and posts to targetOrigin "*" (out)
description:
## Summary

The MCP Apps UI resource (an interactive DataStore table rendered in the host's webview/iframe) communicates with its parent via `postMessage`. Its inbound `message` listener performs no `event.origin` validation, and its outbound messages are sent with target origin `'*'`. Any window/frame able to reach the document can inject data into the table and interfere with the MCP UI handshake, and the UI's own JSON-RPC messages are broadcast without an origin restriction.

## Affected code

`src/resources/datastore-table-ui.ts` (inline HTML):

```js
window.addEventListener('message', function (event) {
  var msg = event.data;                    // no check of event.origin
  if (!msg || typeof msg !== 'object') return;
  if (msg.id !== undefined && _pending[msg.id]) { ... resolve/reject pending MCP request ... }
  ...
  if (data && (data.fields || data.records)) initTable(data);   // renders attacker-supplied data
});

// outbound:
window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: id, method: method, params: params || {} }, '*');
mcpNot: window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc:'2.0', method:method, params:params||{} }, '*');
```

There is no allowlist of accepted origins for inbound messages and no fixed target origin for outbound messages.

## Impact

- **Content spoofing.** A frame that can `postMessage` to the UI can supply
  arbitrary `fields`/`records`, causing the table to render fabricated rows and
  links (e.g. a phishing `__link_url`) that appear to come from the queried
  portal. (Values are HTML-escaped, so this is display spoofing, not script
  injection — no XSS.)
- **Handshake/UX interference.** Because inbound messages matching a pending `id`
  resolve/reject the UI's MCP requests, an attacker frame can spoof responses to
  the `ui/initialize` handshake or otherwise disrupt the panel.
- **Outbound leakage.** Posting to `'*'` means the UI's JSON-RPC messages are
  delivered to whatever the parent origin is; if the resource is ever embedded by
  a context other than the trusted host, those messages leak to it.

Exploitability depends on the host embedding model (in a correct MCP Apps host the
parent is the trusted host, which limits who can message the frame), so this is a
hardening / defense-in-depth issue rather than a directly remotely-triggerable
one — hence Low.

## Proof of concept

- `poc/verify-no-origin-check.mjs` — static confirmation that the listener has no
  origin check and outbound uses `'*'`:

  ```
  [x] validates event.origin             : NO
  [x] outgoing postMessage targetOrigin  : '*' (any)
  RESULT: VULNERABLE
  ```

- `poc/parent-spoof-poc.html` — a page that embeds the UI and injects fabricated
  rows cross-origin with no handshake; the UI renders them.

## Remediation

- Validate `event.origin` against the expected host origin on every inbound
  message; drop messages from other origins.
- Send outbound `postMessage` with an explicit target origin (the host origin
  established at initialize time) instead of `'*'`.
- Optionally, bind to a nonce/channel established during `ui/initialize` so only
  the negotiated host can drive the panel.

summary: TanStack Router: Unauthenticated reflected XSS in TanStack Start server-function responses
description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL to a server function in an affected TanStack Start app. If someone opens the link, the app can return attacker-controlled HTML from its own origin and run the attacker's JavaScript there. The script can access same-origin data available to that visitor and make requests with their authority.

## Cause

The server-function transport can pass request payload fields into internal middleware state instead of limiting them to public input fields. A malformed payload can leave an attacker-controlled result in the error path. Response handling can then treat a response-shaped object as an HTTP response.

## Affected versions

Published versions of `@tanstack/start-server-core`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/solid-start`, and `@tanstack/vue-start` from `1.143.12` up to, but not including, their respective patched versions are affected. The patched versions are `@tanstack/start-server-core@1.169.39`, `@tanstack/react-start@1.168.60`, `@tanstack/solid-start@1.168.57`, and `@tanstack/vue-start@1.168.56`.

## Fix

The fix limits client-supplied server-function input to public fields and validates responses at the server boundary. Upgrade to the corresponding patched package version.

## Temporary mitigations

For the configured server-function path, usually `/_serverFn/*`, an edge or WAF rule can consider blocking requests without the literal `x-tsr-serverFn: true` header and browser document navigations such as `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` or `Accept: text/html`. A restrictive Content Security Policy on server-function responses can provide another browser-side restriction. These are mitigation suggestions, not a complete fix. The header is client-controlled and is not authentication. Test rules against legitimate GET and POST server functions and use a matching version-specific backport where possible.

## Credits

Lovable helped us discover and report this issue. We thank them for their help.

summary: Claude Code: Plugin Hash Pin Bypass Allows Bypass of Hash Pinning
description:
The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

summary: OpenNext Cloudflare: Cache interception can bypass middleware protection for encoded paths
description:
## Summary

When cache interception is enabled, `@opennextjs/cloudflare` can interpret percent-encoded paths differently during middleware matching and cache lookup.

An encoded request may fail to match authorization middleware, then be decoded into the cache key of a protected route. The cached response may consequently be returned without invoking the middleware.

`enableCacheInterception` is disabled by default.

## Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker may retrieve cached content from routes intended to be protected by middleware.

An application is affected when it:

- explicitly enables `enableCacheInterception`;
- relies on middleware for access control; and
- has a matching cached route.

## Details

Middleware matching previously used the encoded request pathname, while cache interception decoded the pathname before selecting a cache entry.

For example, consider an application with:

- middleware matcher `/admin/:path*`;
- middleware returning `401 Authentication required` for `/admin`;
- a statically generated, cached `/admin` route; and
- cache interception enabled:

```ts
export default defineCloudflareConfig({
  incrementalCache: staticAssetsIncrementalCache,
  enableCacheInterception: true,
});
```

An attacker can request:

```http
GET /%61dmin
```

The encoded pathname does not match `/admin/:path*`, so the authorization middleware is not invoked. Cache interception then decodes `%61dmin` to `admin` and may return the cached `/admin` response:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-opennext-cache: HIT

Protected content
```

Malformed paths exposed an additional inconsistency. For example:

```http
GET /%61dmin/%ZZ
```

The previous implementation decoded each segment independently. It decoded `%61dmin` to `admin` but retained the malformed `%ZZ` segment, allowing cache lookup to continue using a partially decoded pathname.

## Patches

The fix aligns encoded-path handling across middleware matching and cache lookup, and rejects malformed paths instead of partially decoding them. See the upstream fixes in [opennextjs-aws#1199](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1199) and [opennextjs-aws#1200](https://github.com/opennextjs/opennextjs-aws/pull/1200).

Users should upgrade to `@opennextjs/cloudflare@1.20.2` or later.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible for an application:

1. Disable cache interception by removing `enableCacheInterception: true`.
2. Enforce authorization inside protected route handlers rather than relying exclusively on middleware.
3. Reject encoded paths for protected routes at a trusted proxy before they reach the Worker.

Adding individual encoded matcher variants is not a complete workaround because pathnames can have multiple equivalent encodings.

summary: AdonisJS HTTP Server: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption and Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
description:
### Description

A Regular Expression Denial of Service vulnerability in the built-in AdonisJS slug route matcher may allow a remote attacker to block the Node.js event loop using a specially crafted URL.

This affects applications using `router.matchers.slug()` on a route parameter reachable by an attacker.

### Details

The regular expression used by `router.matchers.slug()` contains adjacent greedy quantifiers with overlapping character classes:

```regex
/^[^\s-_](?!.*?[-_]{2,})([a-z0-9-\\]{1,})[^\s]*[^-_\s]$/
```

When the matcher receives a long string ending with a character rejected by the final assertion, the regular expression engine must evaluate many possible ways of dividing the input between the overlapping quantifiers before determining that it does not match.

This results in quadratic execution time. Testing measured an approximate complexity of `O(n^1.98)`.

Route matchers are evaluated against attacker-controlled URL segments during routing. Therefore, an unauthenticated attacker can trigger the vulnerable expression by sending a request to a route configured as follows:

```ts
router
  .get('/posts/:slug', handler)
  .where('slug', router.matchers.slug())
```

Routing occurs before route and group middleware. As a result, authentication or rate-limiting middleware attached to the affected route may not prevent exploitation.

The vulnerability is limited to routes that explicitly use the built-in slug matcher.

### Impact

Exploitation requires an application to expose a route using `router.matchers.slug()` with an attacker-controlled parameter.

A specially crafted request can cause excessive CPU consumption and block the Node.js event loop. While the expression is being evaluated, the process cannot serve other requests, including requests to unrelated routes or health-check endpoints.

Only a small number of requests may be required to consume the capacity of a worker. Reverse-proxy request-line limits reduce the maximum processing time of an individual request but do not fully mitigate the vulnerability.

### Patches

Fixes targeting v6 and v7 have been published below.

Users should upgrade to a version that includes the following fix:

- https://github.com/adonisjs/http-server/releases/tag/v9.1.1
- https://github.com/adonisjs/http-server/releases/tag/v8.2.2

cwes.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
